lead: A TRIAC is one three-terminal device that conducts in both directions, so a single TRIAC replaces the pair of antiparallel SCRs in an AC voltage controller and still needs only one trigger network. Delaying its turn-on in each half cycle cuts a slice out of every half wave, and the RMS voltage reaching the load falls smoothly. This is the circuit inside a domestic lamp dimmer, a ceiling-fan regulator, a room heater and a soldering iron — the cheapest way to control AC power from a 230 V, 50 Hz wall socket.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for the TRIAC and DIAC structure, latching and holding current, and Chapter 5.1 for the phase-control waveform and its RMS formula.

blocks.text: A TRIAC is a three-terminal power switch that conducts in both directions. Its two main terminals are MT1 and MT2. MT1 is the reference terminal: the gate voltage and the gate current are always measured with respect to MT1, never with respect to MT2. Inside, the silicon behaves as two SCRs connected in antiparallel that share one gate region.

With MT2 positive with respect to MT1, one SCR path is forward biased and a gate pulse latches it on. In the next half cycle MT2 is negative, the other path is forward biased, and a second pulse latches that one. The load sees alternating current, but each internal path carries only its own half cycle.

items: Latching current I_L: the current that must be flowing when the gate pulse ends for the device to stay on.
Holding current I_H: the current below which a conducting device turns off. It is smaller than I_L and is reached near every zero crossing.
Gate pulse: a few microseconds is enough. After latching the gate has no control, so a continuous gate current only heats the driver.

blocks.text: A triggering quadrant is one combination of the MT2 polarity and the gate current polarity. Two signs give four cases, Q1 to Q4. The same gate pulse does not fire the device equally well in all four.

Triggering is easiest when the gate current flows in the same direction as the MT2 voltage, that is Q1 (MT2 positive, gate positive) and Q3 (MT2 negative, gate negative). The mixed quadrants need more gate current: Q2 is low sensitivity, and Q4 — MT2 negative with a positive gate — is the weakest of all. Some data sheets quote no Q4 gate current at all.

A single-polarity driver, fed from a capacitor or a pulse transformer, must therefore be checked for the quadrant it reaches in each half cycle. The firing angle is set by the trigger network, but the gate pulse polarity has to follow the mains, or the negative half cycle fires late or not at all.

The common dimmer uses a resistor–capacitor network and a DIAC. A potentiometer in series with a fixed resistor, and a capacitor, form a phase-shifting network across MT2 and MT1. The capacitor voltage lags the supply. When it reaches the DIAC breakover voltage, about 30 V, the DIAC snaps on and dumps the capacitor charge into the gate as one sharp pulse.

The potentiometer sets the RC time constant, hence the delay, hence the firing angle α. At minimum resistance the capacitor charges early, α is small and the lamp is bright. At maximum resistance the delay is long, α approaches 180°, and the lamp is dim.

A UJT or a PUT trigger does the same job with a programmable threshold: the capacitor charges through a resistor and discharges through the device into the gate. Both allow a pulse transformer, which isolates the control circuit from the mains. An optotriac with an LED input gives opto-isolated drive straight from a microcontroller pin. A zero-crossing optotriac version holds off until the mains voltage passes near zero, producing the whole-cycle on-off control of Chapter 5.1 with very little switching noise.

A series RC snubber across MT1 and MT2 limits the rate of rise of voltage dv/dt at turn-off. Without it, the fast voltage step injects charge through the junction capacitance and can fire the TRIAC with no gate pulse: the lamp flickers, or the device fails. Typical values are 100 Ω with 100 nF, checked against the device data sheet.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 100 W incandescent lamp through a TRIAC phase controller. The DIAC trigger network is set so the TRIAC fires at α = 90° in every half cycle. Find the lamp resistance, the RMS voltage across the lamp, the RMS current and the power delivered.
steps: Rated lamp data: the lamp is specified for 230 V, 100 W, so at rated conditions R = V²/P = 230²/100 = 52900/100 = 529 Ω.
Supply: V_s = 230 V RMS at 50 Hz, so the peak is 230√2 = 325.3 V and each half cycle lasts 10 ms.
Firing angle: α = 90° = π/2 rad. The TRIAC conducts from α to 180° in each half cycle, so the conduction angle is also 90°.
RMS load voltage from the AC controller formula V_rms = V_s √[(1/π)(π − α + sin2α/2)]. Here sin2α = sin180° = 0, so V_rms = 230 √[(π − π/2)/π] = 230 √0.5 = 230 × 0.707 = 162.61 V.
Power in the lamp: P = V_rms I_rms = V_rms²/R = 162.61²/529 = 26442/529 = 49.98 W, which is half of the 100 W rating, so the lamp runs at half brightness.
Cross-check with the current form: P = I_rms²R = 0.3074² × 529 = 0.0945 × 529 = 49.98 W, the same value.
examples.answer: R = 529 Ω, V_rms = 162.61 V, I_rms = 0.3074 A and P = 49.98 W, that is half brightness at half power.

V = 230 * 0.707

traps: Naming the quadrant from the gate polarity alone. MT2 positive with a positive gate is Q1, but the same positive pulse with MT2 negative is Q4, the least sensitive quadrant.
Believing the gate must stay energised for the whole half cycle. After latching the gate does nothing; the device turns off only when the current falls below the holding current.
Swapping latching current and holding current. Latching current is needed at turn-on while the gate pulse is ending; holding current is the level at which a conducting device drops out.
Curing false triggering by raising the gate resistor. The usual cause is excessive dv/dt, and the cure is an RC snubber and a correct snubber value, not a weaker gate drive.
Using the controlled-rectifier formula V_rms = V_s cos α for a TRIAC dimmer. At α = 90° the dimmer gives 0.707 V_s, not zero.

quiz.q: Name the three terminals of a TRIAC and state which terminal the gate is referred to.
quiz.a: MT1, MT2 and the gate G. The gate current and gate voltage are referred to MT1, not MT2.

quiz.q: Define a triggering quadrant and list Q1 to Q4 by MT2 and gate polarity.
quiz.a: A quadrant is one combination of MT2 polarity and gate current polarity. Q1: MT2 +, gate +. Q2: MT2 +, gate −. Q3: MT2 −, gate −. Q4: MT2 −, gate +.

quiz.q: Why is a gate pulse of a few microseconds enough to keep a TRIAC on for the rest of the half cycle?
quiz.a: The pulse starts the regenerative action inside the device and both internal transistors latch. Once the anode current exceeds the latching current the gate loses control, so the pulse can end. The device stays on until the current falls below the holding current, which happens near the zero crossing.

quiz.q: Why is Q4 the least sensitive triggering quadrant?
quiz.a: In Q4 the gate current polarity opposes the MT2 potential, so the carriers injected at the gate are partly swept the wrong way and are less effective at starting conduction. A larger gate current is needed to reach the latching condition, and some devices are not specified for Q4 operation at all.

quiz.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 100 W lamp through a TRIAC dimmer with α = 60°. Find the RMS voltage across the lamp and the power delivered. The lamp resistance is 529 Ω.
quiz.a: V_rms = V_s √[(1/π)(π − α + sin2α/2)] with α = π/3. π − α = 2.0944 rad, sin120° = 0.8660 so sin2α/2 = 0.4330. Sum = 2.5274; divide by π gives 0.8045; square root gives 0.8969. V_rms = 230 × 0.8969 = 206.3 V. P = 206.3²/529 = 80.4 W.

quiz.q: A microcontroller drives a TRIAC gate through a pulse transformer that delivers only positive pulses. What happens in the negative half cycle and how is it fixed?
quiz.a: With MT2 negative a positive gate pulse fires the device in Q4, its least sensitive quadrant. The same gate current may be too small to latch it, so the negative half cycle fires late or not at all and the load sees DC or flicker. The fix is a driver that reverses the pulse with the mains, so the negative half cycle fires in Q3.

quiz.q: A lamp dimmer works on the bench but flickers when the snubber is removed. Explain.
quiz.a: At turn-off the voltage across MT1–MT2 rises fast. The junction capacitance then injects enough charge to fire the TRIAC with no gate pulse, which is false triggering by dv/dt. The snubber slows the rise and keeps the device off until the next gate pulse.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the TRIAC dimmer is being pushed in two directions: solid-state relays that pack the TRIAC, an optotriac driver and the snubber into one module for heaters and small motors, and back-to-back MOSFET AC switches in smart dimmers and inverter fan regulators, because MOSFETs switch at any phase, need no holding current and handle LED and capacitive loads. TRIAC circuits still dominate the low-cost market, and most design effort now goes into the load: an LED lamp draws narrow current spikes that can keep a TRIAC on or drop it out, so a bleeder and a larger snubber are added. Search for TRIAC quadrants and gate current, DIAC breakover voltage, snubber design for AC switches, and leading-edge phase dimming.
